cards.explanation: The answer is saving him. David asks why God is “…so far from saving me…” and he says it plain. He doesn't dress it up or make it fancy. I think that's the kind of prayer you can only pray when you really need help, friends. And he prays it right when God feels far away.

The answer is False. David says, “I cry out by day, O my God, but You do not answer…” So in this moment, he isn't hearing an answer. He says it honestly, and he keeps talking to God anyway. He also says he has no rest by night, which I think is a hard combination.

The answer is delivered. David says, “In You our fathers trusted; they trusted and You delivered them.” Then the next verse says they cried out and were set free. David is looking back at what God has done before, friends. When you're stuck, a good memory can be the best thing in your pocket.

The answer is rescue. The people who mock David sneer, “He trusts in the LORD, let the LORD deliver him; let the LORD rescue him, since He delights in him.” They're using David's trust as a punchline. It stings, and I think it's meant to. The people laughing in this verse are not the ones to learn from, bakers.

The answer is False. David says, “From birth I was cast upon You; from my mother’s womb You have been my God.” That's from the very start of his life, friends. A crown has nothing to do with it. God has been his God since his mother's womb.

The answer is that trouble is near and no one can help. David says, “Be not far from me, for trouble is near and there is no one to help.” He doesn't ask for anything fancy. He asks God not to be far, because there is no one to help. I think that's a prayer a lot of us have prayed.

The answer is that he is weak and worn out. Water poured out can't be gathered back up, and wax goes soft in the heat. David also says his strength is “…dried up like a potsherd…” (a piece of broken pottery). Put those pictures together, friends, and you see a man who is weak and worn out. I think he's saying he feels drained.

The answer is True. David says, “I can count all my bones; they stare and gloat over me.” That's a hard picture, and I think this part of the psalm is heavy. He's showing how worn down he is, with people staring at him while he suffers. It's a lot, and he says it honestly.

The answer is his clothing. David says, “They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing.” They are dividing his garments among themselves. It's a cold moment, friends, and I think it hurts. Casting lots was a way of choosing who got what, and here it's used on a man's clothing.

The answer is his life. David prays, “Deliver my soul from the sword, my precious life from the power of wild dogs.” He calls it his “precious life.” That's what's on the line, and he asks God to guard it. When you're in that kind of trouble, friends, you ask for the thing that matters most.

The answer is proclaim. David says, “I will proclaim Your name to my brothers; I will praise You in the assembly.” That's not a whisper in the corner. He's going to say it out loud where people can hear. Right after the cry, bakers, here comes the voice.

The answer is False. David says, “You who fear the LORD, praise Him!” He also says, “All offspring of Israel, revere Him!” No priests are singled out. The invitation is for everybody who fears the LORD, friends. I like a guest list that big.

The answer is that the LORD heard his cry for help. David says the LORD “…has not hidden His face from him, but has attended to his cry for help.” That's a reason worth singing about, friends. The one who was crying out was heard. After all those verses of groaning, that's good news.

The answer is the poor. David says, “The poor will eat and be satisfied; those who seek the LORD will praise Him.” They don't just eat, they eat and are satisfied. I think that's a lovely promise to hear, friends.

The answer is True. David says all the families of the nations will bow down before Him. Then he gives the reason: “For dominion belongs to the LORD and He rules over the nations.” The ruling comes first, and the bowing follows. It's a big, wide picture, bakers.

The answer is False. David says, “All the rich of the earth will feast and worship…” They're not left out at all, friends. They get a seat at the feast and join the worship. The line goes on to say that those who go down to the dust will kneel before Him too.

The answer is His righteousness. David says they will “…proclaim His righteousness…” to a people not yet born. The next generation gets told who God is and what He has done. It's a story passed from one group to the next, friends. I think that's the best kind of handoff.
